title: Good ayis are always on assignment: what a domestic-service consultant really sells isn't information
dek: Domestic work is a supply-led industry: good ayis never reach the open market, and the consultant's hard part isn't closing the deal but handling replacements after the sale; both employers and ayis are just pass-throughs for a paycheck.
why: A frontline post-00s domestic-service consultant lays out a neglected essential industry: matching mechanics, pricing, off-platform deals, boundaries — high information density, and the second half is worth more.
who: Dual-income families hiring or about to hire a yuesao or yuer sao, and founders and investors watching domestic services and local life services.
skip: From 1:35:37, the part about the twins family interviewing over picture books is more story than substance — fast-forward.

points.h: Good ayis are always on assignment
points.body: This market has a circulation paradox: ayis with good reviews never reach the open market. She works for one family for two or three years, and the moment she leaves she's referred straight to the next one. The ones actually circulating on the market are usually the ones nobody could be satisfied with, however many families tried. So the industry's core contradiction is supply — where good ayis come from and how they get discovered. A domestic-service company is essentially a human resources company: it has to recruit, train and re-match.

points.h: Every woman in this trade has a story
points.body: The ayi profile clusters in third- and fourth-tier cities and even poor villages, aged 30 to 45, many divorced or single. Live-in sisters spend little time with their own families and give their time to another family. Two obvious traits mark their choice of this work: they like children, and they hunger to earn — not to sit comfortably in the village farming and drinking tea, but to pack up everything they own, buy a green-skin train ticket and squeeze their way to Shanghai.

There has to be a sense of boundaries and tact between ayi and employer — not just toward the ayi, but toward the employer too. Some people spoil the ayi past the line, but people always take a mile when given an inch. More delicate still: a live-in ayi is together with the family 24 hours a day, and may know more about the household's private life than close relatives do — the pressure is heavy. Some moms are doing widow-style parenting with the dad absent, and it's the ayi who keeps the mom company longer, until the two become teammates.

points.h: Employers and ayis are both pass-throughs for a paycheck
points.body: To the employer she looks like a pass-through for a paycheck, and it's the same for the ayi: the money arrives by WeChat transfer each month, and immediately two children's tuition goes out, then the household living expenses — gone just like that. For many yuesao and yuer sao, the income is the most important or even the only source for the family, which is why her role as wife within the family structure is a strong one. That also explains why employers care about the ayi's family background — you're not hiring a company employee, and her stability is directly tied to her family situation.

points.h: How a ten-page job spec doesn't scare the ayi away
points.body: The longest yuesao job spec I've seen ran a full ten pages, at a price that was only the market average. The employer thinks that if every minute is spelled out, the ayi will execute like a robot — but people are emotional. The consultant doesn't forward it directly; she first calls to lay the groundwork by voice: asking about luggage, giving directions, saying the client just wants to know what time you'll arrive, then explaining that company rules require the employer to list requirements and that you can come to me anytime with questions. That way the ayi feels she's been handed a guidebook, not interrogated.

points.h: Closing the deal is easy; replacing someone is the test
points.body: Yuesao bookings are advance orders, while yuer sao jobs are mostly urgent — an ayi can only enter the market after leaving her previous family, so demand is pressing. Many employers assume that whoever is urgently needed must be bad, but often it's the one who was booked in advance who turns out to be the fake. Closing a deal isn't hard for a consultant: as long as the employer has a need and a budget, someone can always be found. The genuinely hard part is long-term after-sales — you can be thrilled during the interview and still, with some probability, be deflated later, and replacing someone is what really tests a consultant's level.

points.h: The hardest case demands insight into the family's core relationship
points.body: The hardest case: a single mother who is a female executive, wanting a daytime child-development companion, but also expecting this person to do housework to cleaning-standard results — while the companion's hourly rate is twice a cleaner's. The consultant dealt with an assistant, and the core need was also shaped by the executive mother. The compromise was cleaners for cleaning and companions for companionship, but the mother still had to be won over. The person finally found was the polar opposite of the original spec — originally under 35 with a bilingual kindergarten teaching background; in the end, a sister close to 50 with an education background and live-in experience.

points.h: Yuesao start at 15,000; yuer sao are priced by age
points.body: In first-tier cities a yuesao's 26-day contract price is generally 15,000 to 16,000 or more; for one with two or three years' experience who has genuinely cared for a newborn, it's basically 15,000 to 20,000. Shanghai rates for yuer sao: beginners from 7,000, experienced hands priced by age, skills and work history, basically 8,000-plus; stack on English, bilingual, early education or driving and it's 10,000-plus. Prices have risen in recent years partly because more highly educated people are entering the trade, and partly because supply still falls short of demand.

points.h: Consensus and trade norms are what this industry lacks most
points.body: The live-in norm is that the ayi brings her own personal items and the employer provides the big items like bedding, but the two sides of the employment relationship haven't formed a consensus yet. Some think it's lovely when an ayi who's been there a long time grows attached and spends her own wages buying things for the baby; others find it too close. A common situation is a mother who is unhappy that the child is too attached to the ayi. The consultant's training says: the person in a household who should be closest to the child is the mom — not the dad, and not the grandparents.

points.h: Young people doing domestic work is long past being a meme
points.body: By the time something becomes a meme, the number of people doing it is already beyond what you'd imagine. The contraction of the education-training industry fed a lot of talent into domestic services; child-development companions are very young, a cohort in their twenties, because jobs are hard to find and this trade provides room and board and responsibility for just one child. After five to eight years of live-in experience, yuying shi and yuesao get older and can't keep up with the kids, and shift toward training-instructor roles. But whether you do yuying shi or child-development companionship, it's very hard to build a three-to-five-year career plan.

quotes.text: For the employer it's like being a pass-through for a paycheck, and for a lot of ayis it's really the same.
Because an ayi is a person — a person isn't a machine, a person is in a state where they'll have emotions.
Closing a deal isn't a hard thing for us — we can always help an employer find someone they're satisfied with, as long as they have a need, right, and a budget. But the hard part usually comes later.
I think right now both sides of the employment relationship haven't really formed this consensus — they haven't yet accumulated to the point of knowing roughly what state this industry is in.
When something has already become a meme, the number of people doing it is already beyond what you'd imagine.
